narrative:
The model predicted a 57.2% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your undergraduate GPA, your LSAT score, and your academic performance in the third year of law school. Your LSAT score and third-year performance were the strongest reasons the model leaned toward predicting failure. Both were noticeably below the typical level seen among students who were accepted. Your lower LSAT score pushed the prediction toward failure because the model has learned that higher scores strongly predict passing the bar. Similarly, finishing in the second decile of your class in year three, compared with an average around the sixth decile for accepted students, also pulled the outcome toward failure.

Your undergraduate GPA was the only one of these three factors that worked in your favor. At 3.10 it was only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, and this modest difference slightly increased the model’s confidence that you might pass. Unfortunately, the positive effect from your GPA was not large enough to outweigh the downward pressure from your LSAT and third-year grades.

You should consider retaking the LSAT and aiming for a meaningfully higher score, or strengthening your academic record if you have additional coursework ahead. Improving either of those areas would likely change the model’s prediction and improve your chances of admission.
